Messages.Author: Derek Ray
Messages.Body:
So there's been a lot of talk lately about whether or not dial-a-vamp
would really be a problem. Whether or not the grouping rule was really
necessary. Why it would be such a bad thing to just play with all of
the vamps, and why the designers were supposedly "too lazy".

Here is an idea of why the grouping rule was necessary, and a brief
attempt to show it, along with a sample deck. Note that this deck was
built in approximately 15 minutes. It has gone through little to no
tuning whatsoever, and as a result is nowhere near as good as it could
be -- it needs both a Presence and Celerity skill card, for example.
But it's pretty solid where it stands. It required no thought to build;
something that I consider to be a Bad Thing to encourage in the game.

I initially generated the list of vampires by filtering on all vampires
with both Presence and Celerity who were also a 5-cap or cheaper. I
then removed all the 4-caps and 5-caps who had (pre cel), and also
removed Itzahk Levine ('cos he's ugly) to get down to 14. I can't tell
right now whether it would be better to either remove one more 3-cap and
Antoinette, OR remove a couple of the 5-caps.

PRE/CEL: Rigby and Brachah (2)
PRE/cel: Ramiel/Mariana (1) and Barth/Jade (3)
pre/CEL: Felicia/Black Cat (1), Victor/Dodd (2), and Steve (3)
pre/cel: Uma Hatch (1), Antoinette duChamp (2), Mazz (3)

The grouping rule would force me to remove either five V:TES vampires
from my crypt, or four CE vampires. I would be forced to replace them
with inferior minions in some fashion; either by pre/cel vamps, or by
more expensive vampires that the deck really can't afford (Sheila
Mezarin and Sela at 6 for the +1 bleeders, or Ian Wallingford and Julian
Sanders for the PRE/CEL, and Suzanne Kadim at 7 for both), OR by
doubling up on Rigby, Brachah, and two of the pre/CEL vamps, which
significantly hurts my chances of getting a shedload of vampires in
play, significantly increases the chance of my getting a duplicate vamp
or a crappy draw, and noticeably restricts the efficency of the deck.

A player with no access to Jyhad/V:TES is at a significant disadvantage
here; he cannot play with Mariana (4-cap!), Black Cat (huge vamp in this
deck), or Felicia (distinct vamp with pre/CEL, the preferred discipline
set). He'll have to backfill somewhere and make his deck weaker. This
demonstrates quite well why the grouping rule benefits new players.

I don't think the deck is broken right now without the grouping rule; it
should operate more or less as advertised, and has its share of holes.
I think that if I or anyone else spent the time tuning it, though, it
can be an EXTREMELY solid example of its type.

What the deck DOES demonstrate is why any new vampires added without a
grouping rule surely WOULD either break the game or even more glaringly
exaggerate the difference between old and new players. Take, for
example, Black Cat. A new player is already at a disadvantage here; he
doesn't have her, and you almost want 3 of her in the deck. So say you
print a new 5-cap Brujah with her stats. Great! I can now use both
Black Cat and this new Brujah and get BOTH in play; the new player
hasn't caught up to me yet, and in fact is trailing further behind,
since he has to duplicate his crypt to get a -1 pool equipper out and I
still don't.

The other question is: how do you add a vampire with pre CEL or PRE
cel? If the most likely target for group 4 vamps is a new
Sabbat-related expansion, that gives you two clans (!Tories and !Brujah)
who have PRE CEL as their in-clan disciplines. Do you totally avoid
printing a 5-cap with pre/CEL or CEL/pre? You certainly don't want to,
but otherwise you really do start to degenerate badly.

So, for your consideration: some bruise-and-sleaze.

financial decision, then I suppose I begrudgingly support it. But I really
don't think it was. I think that the layout change was an aesthetic decision
that was unfortunately made by blind monkeys with no sense of taste or

strong an opinion about the design decision, as it's not obviously bad for the

either. I just personally don't really like it.

I definitely get the blind monkeys part. As for DS / AH, at least some of
those guys were from the official cannon and, if there was any sort of
financial arrangement, it was probably WotC paying WW for the use of their

batch of vamps that totally conflicted with the cannon when the game first
appeared and suspected that that, too, was a decision made on the basis of
saving money.

Actually, thinking about it, making sure that everything currently being
printed makes sense for WW in the sense that cannon vamps are more familiar
to people who play the RPG and therefore more likely to entice them into
making the jump into VtES.

Messages.Author: Halcyan 2

My guesses.

>I definitely get the blind monkeys part. As for DS / AH, at least some of
>those guys were from the official cannon and, if there was any sort of
>financial arrangement, it was probably WotC paying WW for the use of their
>material. I often wondered at the sheer weirdness of WotC just making up a
>batch of vamps that totally conflicted with the cannon when the game first
>appeared and suspected that that, too, was a decision made on the basis of
>saving money.

Canon vampires would have taken more time to do and would have strait-jacketed
the design and balance by Richard Garfield. Knowing that "that other game" had
been a hit and eager to quickly cash in on the success before the market became
too saturated, creating vampires would have been much faster than carefully
making sure everything agreed. And indeed, Jyhad was one of the earlier CCG's
out there if I recall correctly.

>Actually, thinking about it, making sure that everything currently being
>printed makes sense for WW in the sense that cannon vamps are more familiar
>to people who play the RPG and therefore more likely to entice them into
>making the jump into VtES.

As for White Wolf, I sincerely doubt they could even have begun to suspect that
VTES would grow and evolve into what it has become today. CCG's was still a
relatively new industry back then (and still is relatively speaking). White
Wolf probably didn't know squat about CCG's but saw how much money they could
rake in. So they let WotC, which had proven successes, take over the reins. For
many in the gaming industry, the more immediate future is much more worrisome
than the effects and consequences almost 10 years down the line...

Halcyan 2

The game survived for 5 years without product on the shelves. I think
that's pretty good proof right there.

We have around 20 people in our play group, and they buy 90% of their
cards online. Most of us buy online exclusively. Almost everyone of
college age, the primary source of new players, has access to the
internet and can buy online. Every player I know, other than the ones
that started with the original Jyhad set, was recruited by another
player. None of them started playing by picking up a pack of cards in
a store and finding someone else to play with.

provide a venue for playing. Most stores these days in America have
large play areas. With so many people buying off the internet, I'm not
sure how long they'll continue providing free play space (I buy comics
at our shop, so I don't feel like I'm not contributing to their bottom
line). But the product being on store shelves is largely irrelevant to
the core player base of VTES.

JSpektr

Excellent. So let's take the concept of "making people want what you're
selling" for a moment, shall we, because whether or not you think it is,
a certain amount of market research IS necessary to get people to want
what you're selling. I don't think you're foolish enough to believe

start from an initial point: NEW PLAYERS ARE MANDATORY. Now, where to

material, do not care what the vampires are named, as long as they're
not something like "BART SIMPSON". So the name choice has no effect on
making non-RPGers want what they're selling.

People who DO play the RPG and read the source material are likely to
find it appealing to play with a vampire they recognize, especially one
who shares characteristics from the source material (menele/helena, for
example). So the name choice here has a positive effect as regards
"making them want what is being sold".

I don't see any circumstances where the name choice could have a
negative effect, except one: If most of the vampires in this set are
just reprints of V:TES vamps, I (and most other old players) don't even
consider buying ANY of it, because now it has NO appeal.

>selling is one thing. Marketing, in the sense of tricking them into buying it,
>is sometimes successful, but often turns away a lot of people who have half a
>brain in their head. I suppose people like you prefer to be tricked?

What implies trickery about choosing names that are familiar to people
who have demonstrated they already like things dark and vampiric? Why
would it be a bad idea to try to draw new players from the LARP and
other V:tM crowds?

Marketing is more successful than you ever realize. It's STUPID
marketing that fails, and that kind is spottable right off the bat.

>WW may exist simply to milk money out of unwitting fools. And if so, they have
>every right to. But even if that's true, the unwitting fools have the right to
>(assuming they become witting fools) be upset about it. Personally, I think

to understand that success doesn't happen without a great deal of

involve trickery or anything under-the-table, nor does it involve trying
to "rip consumers off"; and often the most successful companies are the
ones who figure out how to get people to buy what they're selling while
ALSO doing lots of things that the consumer wants. But failure to pay
attention to the bottom line is a sure route to, well... failure.

I don't consider the population of the game at the time WW picked it up
to be "surviving" -- I consider it to be "a bunch of die-hards who were
barely hanging on". If WW hadn't picked the game up, it would've been
history soon after as people got bored and found newer toys that were
still supported.

That core player base will, over time, diminish. If it is not being
replaced by new players constantly, the game will die. The best source
of new players remains the retail shops; people can see others having
fun playing, see that the game looks "cool", and be recruited on the
spot. If they're told that they have to go order cards off the Internet
(probably in bulk, mind you) to even start, they're liable to shrug and
just wander away to buy a handful of HeroClix. On the other hand, if
they can walk up front, buy a starter deck, play a game... and then walk
up front again later and buy a handful of boosters... NOW there's a much
better chance they'll stick around.

Overall I agree with your assessment. However, I do have to point out the
potential problem that seducing the RPG players might actually backfire, if the
canon vampires aren't created properly.

The RPG-obsessed might get annoyed when this vampire doesn't have this title
which Book XXX clearly states he does (Alfred Benezri and Archbishop of
Montreal for example). And then you get issues of not matching disciplines
(hey! Brujah Vampire XXX doesn't have any potence, celerity, or presence. She
actually has Auspex 6, Daimonon 7, and Melpominee 5 so she should have AUS DAI
MEL instead of the CEL POT PRE). Some people might get dissatisfied or annoyed
by such inaccurate portrayals and may be oblivious to the fact that the CCG
cannot be a simple carbon-copy of the RPG.

On the other hand however, you also have another problem, something which Mr.
Abrasive (Chris Berger) and I actually agree on. It's fine if you create crypt
cards based on (not necessarily exact duplicates) of canon vampires. However,
from the Camarilla Set, it *seems* like White Wolf is just creating crypt cards
and then just pasting the name of some canon character on to the title. I'm not
that much of a stickler for RPG details, but even I have to admit that quite
some things are out of whack. Take for example Dr. Douglas Netchurch and Maris
Streck who are supposed to be explicit exceptions of Malkavians who don't have
Dementation. (And I also still have no idea where they came up with Vicissitude
for a discipline point for Virstania). I mean, a 6-cap Malkavian like Netchurch
was definitely an important, solid vampire for the Malkavians. But the fact
that they simply stuck his name on to the card kind of smacks of desperation
IMO. Don't get me wrong, there are plenty examples of crypt cards that are
excellent representatives of the RPG character. But there are also plenty of
cards that just leave me scratching my head, wondering "did I miss something?",
and trying to figure out why it seems like names were picked out at random.
"Hey there, I just created some 6-cap Ventrue, give me a name!" ::Reaches into
hat full of names from various sourcebooks:: "Okay, got one!"

Halcyan 2

just randomly assign Disciplines to vampires and forget about this
clan thing? ;)

> I'm not that much of a stickler for RPG details, but even I have to admit that quite
> some things are out of whack. Take for example Dr. Douglas Netchurch and Maris
> Streck who are supposed to be explicit exceptions of Malkavians who don't have
> Dementation.

Sure, sometimes vampires are different in VTE than V:tM. I figur that
this is generally because a perfect "translation" would have critical
flaws that don't matter in V:tM (eg, the Malkav justicar lacking a
clan Discipline), or because a character would be too powerful for
it's generation/capacity (eg, Lithrac isn't a full archon and doesn't
have any Celerity), or because the VTEs rules prohibit it (eg,
Sarrasine can't hold a Camarilla title).

Generally these are minor things; if a character has major issues (the
mythical AUS DAI MEL Brujah, for example) then they just don't get
converted.

Chris, this is blatant naivete in its most harmful, damaging form. It's
a histrionic, hyperbolic misstatement of reality, and it reminds me of
the rhetoric Linux and MS zealots use attempting to defend and/or
promote their respective products, and I wouldn't want to leave FreeBSD
zealots out either, come to think of it.

Some marketers are Evil and Must Be Destroyed, yes. However, there is
an awful lot of good that comes out of product research as well. To
paint everyone working in marketing with the same "demonic" brush is
amusing and makes great fodder for "Dilbert" comics, but the reality of
it isn't anywhere near this. I suspect you actually know this, much
like I suspect those linux/MS zealots of not being such damn fools as
they are. I would appreciate it if you wouldn't carry on this way, as
it doesn't do us or our cause any help and doesn't actually say much.

Besides, I don't think you really meant to say that jspektr is soulless,
doesn't respect vision or integrity, and would put naked pictures of his
own mother on packaging. Though he might.

>young children, most people wouldn't care, but supporters of child-flaying
>would increase profit-margins by nearly 1%!!!" Maybe you don't know these
>people or what they're capable of. But more likely you are one of them (did
>you go to a liberal arts school, Derek?) and have deluded yourself that

No, Chris, I didn't go to college. I've worked in the technical
industry since I was 18. My first job was a technical support/data
entry position with a small law firm. I have since worked for 4
different Fortune 500 class companies (one privately held), and a couple
other small ones along the way. I've even spent some time at a
dot-bomb, although I successfully got out prior to losing my life
savings there upon realizing that it was bound to fail (not just no
marketing, but no product that would appeal to anyone).

I'm about to turn 31. This means I've been doing this shit for 13 years
(technically 11, because I took a couple years off playing pool). What
THAT means that I actually know something about what I'm talking, and
frankly, Chris, I am CERTAIN that you do not have the kind of experience
I do dealing with issues like this. You strike me as about 26, recently
graduated from college, and recently introduced to the fact that life
isn't pretty and corporations suck. They always have, and always will.
But the suckage was derived from goodness at one point, and not
everything sucks the same way.

>marketing isn't evil. The simple fact that WW used vampires from canon isn't
>something I'm upset with. I think the canon and the storyline ruined the RPG
>and threatens to ruin the CCG, but that's a different discussion entirely. The
>reason that I didn't want to discuss the topic any further was in deference to
>Godwin's Law. The moment anyone mentions anything about nazis, the topic will
>no longer be fruitful. And even the nazis bowed down before the evil might of
>marketing and propaganda.

This is a load of more histrionic, hyperbolic crap. I suggest you refer
to the actual story behind Godwin's Law, and attempts to invoke it
incorrectly.

>> What implies trickery about choosing names that are familiar to people
>> who have demonstrated they already like things dark and vampiric? Why
>> would it be a bad idea to try to draw new players from the LARP and
>> other V:tM crowds?
>>
>Nothing, but the mention of marketing research buzz-words implies trickery.
>That's what those buzz-words were invented for.

No, Chris. Those words were invented to describe things that there
weren't any words for. They probably aren't the best words, and using
the buzzwords without providing any substance underneath is the hallmark
of trickery, but I don't see a problem with calling a thing by its right
name.

>> I don't see that it involves ripping money off from anyone. I think you
>> are also displaying a bit of naivete here yourself, frankly. You need
>> to understand that success doesn't happen without a great deal of
>> attention to the bottom line. That attention doesn't automatically
>> involve trickery or anything under-the-table, nor does it involve trying
>> to "rip consumers off"; and often the most successful companies are the
>> ones who figure out how to get people to buy what they're selling while
>> ALSO doing lots of things that the consumer wants. But failure to pay
>> attention to the bottom line is a sure route to, well... failure.
>>
>But when it does involve trickery, it is no longer in the interests of the
>consumers. You seem to be implying that no money can ever be made without such
>trickery. Again, I understand that there is a difference between advertisement
>and marketeering, and I suppose I wouldn't have flown off the handle if you
>hadn't come in with the stupid buzz-words. The language of evil.

This focus on "evil" is out of hand, Chris. I'm sorry Marketing stole
your wife and raped your dog, or whatever they did to you. But holding
a grudge against the whole thing forever is so very, very...
User-Friendlyesque. I mean, it's like it's the new fad to be a
technical person and hate marketing or something.

>That's a little cold. Coming down on a guy because the computer industry is
>down and the start-up I worked for owes me enough money to buy my own boat...

We all have our tales, Chris. If you buy me a beer maybe I'll share
mine with you someday.

>(and I blame it all on incompetent marketeers, partially because they spent all
>their time in meetings trying to figure out shortcuts for ripping off customers
>instead of selling the program, and partially because a lot of their lies were
>immediately visible to product reviewers - "of course it doesn't do that! what
>do you mean our literature says it does?") But since you're so concerned, I
>moved back outta the p's house in April.

Really? I don't think you're putting the blame in the right place at
all, although it may well have been true for your company that Marketing
sent the whole thing into the tank; it's something they're certainly
capable of.

I think you should put the blame for the INDUSTRY dropping, however, on
all the broom-pushers who worked on their home computer for 3 months and
then went out and got jobs paying $80k a year claiming they were
"systems administrators"... and these people didn't even know what DNS
was, much less how to configure it. All those people who read "C++ for
Dummies" and then got jobs as programmers. All those people who read a
few backs of magazines and then got jobs as CIOs.

I think that the industry fell in the toilet upon the rest of the world
realizing that the broom-pushers were taking them for a ride, had been
all along, and that they really didn't know shit about the technology
that everyone was claiming was the greatest; that all the yoyos who
memorized the cheat sheet to an MCSE were, in fact, still just yoyos. I
think there was a huge backlash related to anything technological, and I
don't blame them either; I was really tired of dealing with "Minesweeper
Consultants and Solitaire Experts" myself.

The broom-pushers are still being weeded out of the industry. We won't
see a significant upturn until they're all back to being broom-pushers,
and let the rest of us be trusted again. In the meantime, it's a hard
road to hoe for all of us.

>Oh wait... you weren't concerned at all, were you? You were just being
>facetious. I get it now, you're saying I'm a loser. Funny joke. How wily and
>clever you are, Derek Rey.

Sorry I didn't bite on your sob story, Chris Burger. Also sorry I
didn't bother doing the stalking/research necessary to find out that it
might have been true at some point before speaking. Well, not really.

>> fun playing, see that the game looks "cool", and be recruited on the
>> spot. If they're told that they have to go order cards off the Internet
>> (probably in bulk, mind you) to even start, they're liable to shrug and
>
>All our new players have been recruited, and not in comic shops,
>though a few pre-existing players found us in comic shops. Players
>have been told they should buy cards on the internet, every single one
>of them thought that was fine, and prefered it to buying at retail.

We have countless people (ex-players) who drop by the retail store, see
us playing, and say things like "Hey, I used to play that game. I
didn't know anyone still played it!", along with other cute statements
like "So are the Malkavians still totally broken?"

>Do you have actual, direct experience with this phenomena, or are you
>just creating suppositions? So far real life events in St. Louis
>demonstrate the opposite to your claims. I'm willing to admit St.
>Louis may not be typical, but at the least it shows your claims are
>not necessarily true. At the most it shows they are entirely false.

Yeah, I have plenty of direct experience with this phenomena. We can't
get a number of players to play BECAUSE they can't buy in the shops.
They say "We don't want to go buying all those cards and find out we
don't like the game... can't we just get like a few or something?"...
which can be a real bitch when the cards aren't in the store at all. We
can offer them our decks, but they don't seem to go for that, they want
to make something themselves. Fine.

So we have contrary direct experience. Now, apply Occam's razor and
Derek's Law Of Laziness (given equal options, people will seek the
course involving least effort) and we get the conclusions above. I
don't see the flaw here, nor do I believe there is one; and I have to
say that a game **requiring** that much active recruitment from its
pre-existing playerbase is as dead as it gets, and we've just got a
stick up its bum and wiggling it around to make it seem live.
